rationale: I read the complete held EO 9301 (8 FR 1825, Feb. 9, 1943, 'Establishing a Minimum Wartime Work-Week of Forty-Eight Hours'): para. 1 sets the 48-hour minimum workweek 'for the duration of the war', paras. 2-4 bind agencies and contractors and give the War Manpower Commission Chairman interpretive and regulatory power, para. 5 is a non-conflict clause for hours and wage laws. It has no dated term; the 'duration of the war' wording is the only own-term. I read the complete held EO 9607 (10 FR, Aug. 31, 1945, 'Revoking Executive Order 9301 of February 9, 1943'): its one operative sentence orders that 'Executive Order 9301 of February 9, 1943, establishing a minimum wartime workweek of forty-eight hours, be, and it is hereby, revoked', with no condition, exception or savings language, so the whole order ended on signing, Aug. 30, 1945. D6 self-check: the catalog 'See: EO 9333' cross-reference is a mismatch (EO 9333 is a Civil Service Schedule A amendment; I read the held pages). The only other held order that names EO 9301 is EO 9332 (Solid Fuels Administration for War, Apr. 19, 1943), which merely says solid-fuels directives must not conflict with WMC directives issued under EO 9301 and amends nothing; it predates the revocation and cannot revive the order. Other numeric hits in the corpus (EO 10366, 10648) are Federal Register page numbers. No held later instrument revives or re-enacts the workweek rule. The 'duration of the war' term could not have ended before the Aug. 30, 1945 revocation on any reading that I can support from the held record (formal war-termination proclamations came later), so no earlier own-term ending changes the NO. Provisional NO hypothesis only.
